title: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Certainly no clear line of demarcation has as yet been drawn between species and sub-species—that is, the forms which in the opinion of some naturalists come very near to, but do not quite arrive at the rank of species; or, again, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Doubtful species”. Scope: plants and animals in nature

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Massive public taxonomic and sequence datasets directly reveal overlap among ranks. Circularity limits some comparisons, but independent reproductive and genomic metrics can provide a decisive test of a universal clear line.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compile genetic, morphological and reproductive distances from individuals through named varieties, subspecies and species, and test whether any universal discontinuity separates ranks. Continuous overlapping distance distributions support the claim; a robust cross-taxon gap refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Different species concepts imply different boundaries.

Taxonomic ranks are partly assigned using the same traits.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.65
data existence: 0.91
operationalizability: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public barcodes, sequences, and rank catalogues already support a distance-continuum test that many groups have effectively received. Adequacy is high for animal species boundaries and weaker for plants and for the fine end of individual differences, which is part of the stated series. The analysis is standard, and the main limit is that a gap at one rank in one kingdom would refute the fully universal reading without settling every taxon.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Build distributions of genetic and phenotypic distance for pairs ranked as individual variants, varieties, subspecies, and species. A single overlapping continuum would support the absence of a clear line; a repeatable gap between adjacent ranks, stable across groups, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Barcode libraries sample species much more densely than the variety-to-individual end of the series.

A gap in animals can coexist with overlap in plants, so the universal wording can fail in one kingdom and hold in another.

Rank labels are partly conventional, so the test recycles taxonomic practice unless distances are computed first and ranks applied after.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.72
data existence: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.68
discriminating power: 0.6
